public import Mathlib.Data.Nat.Squarefree

@[expose] public section

/-!
# Primitive elements of a set with respect to divisibility

An element `n` is *primitive* in a set `S ⊆ ℕ` if `n ∈ S` and no proper divisor of `n` is in `S`.

This concept appears naturally when studying sequences closed under "divisor inheritance" -
if every member `n` of a sequence has the property that `m * n` is also in the sequence
for coprime `m`, then the primitive elements generate the entire sequence.

## Main definitions

* `Set.IsPrimitive`: A natural number `n` is primitive in `S` if `n ∈ S` and
  `n.properDivisors` is disjoint from `S`.
* `Set.primitives`: The set of primitive elements of `S`.

## Main results

* `Set.IsPrimitive.mem`: A primitive element is in the set.
* `Set.IsPrimitive.not_mem_of_properDivisor`: Proper divisors of a primitive element are not
  in the set.
* `Set.one_isPrimitive_iff`: `1` is primitive in `S` iff `1 ∈ S`.
* `Set.prime_isPrimitive_iff`: A prime `p` is primitive in `S` iff `p ∈ S` and `1 ∉ S`.
-/

namespace Set

/-- An element `n` is *primitive* in a set `S ⊆ ℕ` if `n ∈ S` and no proper divisor of `n`
is in `S`. -/
def IsPrimitive (S : Set ℕ) (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  n ∈ S ∧ Disjoint (n.properDivisors : Set ℕ) S

/-- The set of primitive elements of `S`. -/
def primitives (S : Set ℕ) : Set ℕ :=
  {n | S.IsPrimitive n}

theorem IsPrimitive.mem {S : Set ℕ} {n : ℕ} (h : S.IsPrimitive n) : n ∈ S := h.1

theorem IsPrimitive.disjoint_properDivisors {S : Set ℕ} {n : ℕ} (h : S.IsPrimitive n) :
    Disjoint (n.properDivisors : Set ℕ) S := h.2

theorem IsPrimitive.not_mem_of_properDivisor {S : Set ℕ} {n d : ℕ} (h : S.IsPrimitive n)
    (hd : d ∈ n.properDivisors) : d ∉ S :=
  Set.disjoint_left.mp h.2 hd

theorem IsPrimitive.not_mem_of_dvd_of_lt {S : Set ℕ} {n d : ℕ} (h : S.IsPrimitive n)
    (hdvd : d ∣ n) (hlt : d < n) : d ∉ S :=
  h.not_mem_of_properDivisor (Nat.mem_properDivisors.mpr ⟨hdvd, hlt⟩)

theorem isPrimitive_iff {S : Set ℕ} {n : ℕ} :
    S.IsPrimitive n ↔ n ∈ S ∧ ∀ d ∈ n.properDivisors, d ∉ S := by
  simp only [IsPrimitive, Set.disjoint_left, Finset.mem_coe]

theorem isPrimitive_iff' {S : Set ℕ} {n : ℕ} (_hn : 0 < n) :
    S.IsPrimitive n ↔ n ∈ S ∧ ∀ d, d ∣ n → d < n → d ∉ S := by
  rw [isPrimitive_iff]
  constructor <;> intro ⟨hmem, hdiv⟩
  · exact ⟨hmem, fun d hd hlt => hdiv d (Nat.mem_properDivisors.mpr ⟨hd, hlt⟩)⟩
  · exact ⟨hmem, fun d hd => hdiv d (Nat.mem_properDivisors.mp hd).1 (Nat.mem_properDivisors.mp hd).2⟩

theorem mem_primitives_iff {S : Set ℕ} {n : ℕ} : n ∈ S.primitives ↔ S.IsPrimitive n := Iff.rfl

@[simp]
theorem primitives_subset {S : Set ℕ} : S.primitives ⊆ S := fun _ h => h.mem

theorem one_isPrimitive_iff {S : Set ℕ} : S.IsPrimitive 1 ↔ 1 ∈ S := by
  simp [isPrimitive_iff, Nat.properDivisors_one]

theorem prime_isPrimitive_iff {S : Set ℕ} {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) :
    S.IsPrimitive p ↔ p ∈ S ∧ 1 ∉ S := by
  simp [isPrimitive_iff, hp.properDivisors]

end Set

findings.description: At n = 0, the definition does not express the advertised absence of proper divisors in S. Lines 51–52 use Nat.properDivisors, whose value at 0 is the default ∅. Thus S.IsPrimitive 0 ↔ 0 ∈ S, irrespective of other divisors in S. In Lean I proved ({0, 2} : Set ℕ).IsPrimitive 0, although 2 belongs to that set, 2 ∣ 0, and 2 ≠ 0. In particular, Set.primitives inherits the error: ({0, 2} : Set ℕ).primitives = {0, 2}, whereas its divisibility-minimal elements are just {2}. Neither definition restricts its domain to positive integers.
findings.source_evidence: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisor, defines a proper divisor as “A positive divisor of n that is different from n”; https://mathworld.wolfram.com/ProperDivisor.html gives the same convention. Mathlib/NumberTheory/Divisors.lean explicitly warns that 0 has infinitely many divisors and that properDivisors 0 = ∅ is a convention necessitated by the Finset representation. The library's unqualified description of primitivity on S ⊆ ℕ does not account for that exception.
findings.suggested_fix: For divisibility primitivity on all of ℕ, define IsPrimitive S n := n ∈ S ∧ ∀ d, d ∣ n → d ≠ n → d ∉ S (equivalently, n ∈ S ∧ ∀ d ∈ S, d ∣ n → d = n). Restrict the finite-proper-divisor characterization Set.isPrimitive_iff to n > 0. Alternatively, if only positive integers are intended, explicitly require 0 < n in the definition and document that restriction. Set.primitives will inherit the repair. The existing OEIS use is unchanged because its membership predicate already implies positivity.

reformulations.difference: Uses n : ℕ and the library's finite-proper-divisor predicate rather than explicitly quantifying over distinct divisors of a positive integer.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Here the zero discrepancy is unreachable: IsPrimitiveTerm n implies A n, and A n includes 0 < n. For positive n, d ∣ n implies d ≤ n, so d ≠ n is equivalent to d < n. I proved IsPrimitiveTerm n ↔ A n ∧ ∀ d, d ∣ n → d ≠ n → ¬ A d. Therefore this use faithfully captures the OEIS definition, and no downstream wrong_definition finding is warranted.

reformulations.difference: The Lean decomposition applies to every sequence member, whereas the OEIS comment states it for “all the other terms,” after discussing primitive terms.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For a primitive term n, take m = n and s = 1: 1 is squarefree, n is coprime to 1, and n = n * 1. Thus extending the decomposition to primitive terms adds only an automatically satisfied case. I proved the equivalence between the universal statement and its restriction to non-primitive terms without using any admitted problem theorem.

Restricted Set.isPrimitive_iff to positive inputs and updated the affected proofs and documentation. The edited file compiles without warnings, and regression tests verify the zero case and agreement with the previous definition on positive inputs. module


public import Mathlib.Data.Nat.Squarefree

@[expose] public section

/-!
# Primitive elements of a set with respect to divisibility

An element `n` is *primitive* in a set `S ⊆ ℕ` if `n ∈ S` and no proper divisor of `n` is in `S`.
In particular, `0` is primitive in `S` exactly when `S = {0}`.

This concept appears naturally when studying sequences closed under "divisor inheritance" -
if every member `n` of a sequence has the property that `m * n` is also in the sequence
for coprime `m`, then the primitive elements generate the entire sequence.

## Main definitions

* `Set.IsPrimitive`: A natural number `n` is primitive in `S` if `n ∈ S` and
  no distinct element of `S` divides `n`.
* `Set.primitives`: The set of primitive elements of `S`.

## Main results

* `Set.IsPrimitive.mem`: A primitive element is in the set.
* `Set.IsPrimitive.not_mem_of_properDivisor`: Proper divisors of a primitive element are not
  in the set.
* `Set.one_isPrimitive_iff`: `1` is primitive in `S` iff `1 ∈ S`.
* `Set.prime_isPrimitive_iff`: A prime `p` is primitive in `S` iff `p ∈ S` and `1 ∉ S`.
-/

namespace Set

/-- An element `n` is *primitive* in a set `S ⊆ ℕ` if `n ∈ S` and no proper divisor of `n`
is in `S`. -/
def IsPrimitive (S : Set ℕ) (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  n ∈ S ∧ ∀ d, d ∣ n → d ≠ n → d ∉ S

/-- The set of primitive elements of `S`. -/
def primitives (S : Set ℕ) : Set ℕ :=
  {n | S.IsPrimitive n}

theorem IsPrimitive.mem {S : Set ℕ} {n : ℕ} (h : S.IsPrimitive n) : n ∈ S := h.1

theorem IsPrimitive.disjoint_properDivisors {S : Set ℕ} {n : ℕ} (h : S.IsPrimitive n) :
    Disjoint (n.properDivisors : Set ℕ) S :=
  Set.disjoint_left.mpr fun _ hd =>
    h.2 _ (Nat.mem_properDivisors.mp hd).1 (Nat.mem_properDivisors.mp hd).2.ne

theorem IsPrimitive.not_mem_of_properDivisor {S : Set ℕ} {n d : ℕ} (h : S.IsPrimitive n)
    (hd : d ∈ n.properDivisors) : d ∉ S :=
  Set.disjoint_left.mp h.disjoint_properDivisors hd

theorem IsPrimitive.not_mem_of_dvd_of_lt {S : Set ℕ} {n d : ℕ} (h : S.IsPrimitive n)
    (hdvd : d ∣ n) (hlt : d < n) : d ∉ S :=
  h.not_mem_of_properDivisor (Nat.mem_properDivisors.mpr ⟨hdvd, hlt⟩)

/-- The finite-proper-divisor characterization of primitivity for a positive number. -/
theorem isPrimitive_iff {S : Set ℕ} {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) :
    S.IsPrimitive n ↔ n ∈ S ∧ ∀ d ∈ n.properDivisors, d ∉ S := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    exact ⟨h.mem, fun _ hd => h.not_mem_of_properDivisor hd⟩
  · rintro ⟨hmem, hdiv⟩
    refine ⟨hmem, fun d hdvd hne => ?_⟩
    exact hdiv d (Nat.mem_properDivisors.mpr
      ⟨hdvd, lt_of_le_of_ne (Nat.le_of_dvd hn hdvd) hne⟩)

theorem isPrimitive_iff' {S : Set ℕ} {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) :
    S.IsPrimitive n ↔ n ∈ S ∧ ∀ d, d ∣ n → d < n → d ∉ S := by
  rw [isPrimitive_iff hn]
  constructor <;> intro ⟨hmem, hdiv⟩
  · exact ⟨hmem, fun d hd hlt => hdiv d (Nat.mem_properDivisors.mpr ⟨hd, hlt⟩)⟩
  · exact ⟨hmem, fun d hd => hdiv d (Nat.mem_properDivisors.mp hd).1 (Nat.mem_properDivisors.mp hd).2⟩

theorem mem_primitives_iff {S : Set ℕ} {n : ℕ} : n ∈ S.primitives ↔ S.IsPrimitive n := Iff.rfl

@[simp]
theorem primitives_subset {S : Set ℕ} : S.primitives ⊆ S := fun _ h => h.mem

theorem one_isPrimitive_iff {S : Set ℕ} : S.IsPrimitive 1 ↔ 1 ∈ S := by
  simp [isPrimitive_iff Nat.zero_lt_one, Nat.properDivisors_one]

theorem prime_isPrimitive_iff {S : Set ℕ} {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) :
    S.IsPrimitive p ↔ p ∈ S ∧ 1 ∉ S := by
  simp [isPrimitive_iff hp.pos, hp.properDivisors]

end Set
